references_named: Ewald Hering, opponent-process theory of colour vision
rationale: The work is a strong conceptual piece: the timed two-state surface (negative flag → blank field) enacts the opponent-process afterimage as the artwork itself, with the mechanism being the argument (P1). It cleanly answers Johns's Flag and the afterimage-flag demonstration, double-codes as optical trick and conceptual argument (P7), and stages chance/order via random nation/angle against deterministic retinal physics (P5). However, G6 fails: the candidate is materially identical to the already-catalogued 'Afterimage (Not on This Page)' (2026) — same title, same Johns/Hering references, same mechanism, same per-visit random flag in negative with 20s fixation and crossfade to neutral field. This is a duplicate of an existing catalogue entry, not a new work.
reservations: G6 fails: this is the same work as the catalogued 'Afterimage (Not on This Page)' (2026). The candidate meta.json, motivation, and index.html match the existing entry in title, references, mechanism, and execution. No materially distinct source, mechanism, or argument is offered.
revision_suggestion: To pass G6, propose a genuinely distinct afterimage-based work: e.g., a different source artwork (not Johns's Flag), a different physiological phenomenon (not opponent-process), a different timed structure (not 20s fixation + crossfade), or a different found-object (not national flags). Alternatively, develop the Johns-afterimage idea into a new mechanism — e.g., afterimage as a function of scroll velocity, or as a function of viewport size, or paired with a different reference (Albers's Interaction of Color, or Anni Albers, or the Ben-Day dot tradition).
